background.title: What a business is for
background.html:
A business exists to provide goods (things you can touch) or services (things done for you) that people want, and customers pay for them. If more money comes in than goes out, the owners earn a reward for their effort and their risk.

Not every organisation is after money for its owners. State schools, public hospitals and charities also use people, money and buildings to provide something. The differences are who owns them and what happens to any money left over: that is section 1.2.

Every business has the same four jobs to do: look after the people (human resources), the money (finance), the customers (marketing) and making the product (operations).

background.title: Revenue, costs and profit
background.html:
Three money words you will use in every unit:

  • Revenue: all the money from sales. Price × number sold.
  • Costs: all the money paid out: materials, wages, rent, electricity, interest on loans. The everyday costs of running the business are its operating costs.
  • Profit = revenue − costs. If costs are bigger, it is a loss.

Example: a juice stall sells 500 cups at $3. Revenue = 500 × $3 = $1 500. Fruit, cups, a helper's pay and the pitch cost $1 100. Profit = 1 500 − 1 100 = $400.

Revenue is not profit. A firm with high sales can still lose money if its costs are even higher, and profit often falls in a recession, when customers spend less.

background.title: Owning a company: shares and shareholders
background.html:
A company's ownership is split into equal parts called shares. Whoever holds shares is a shareholder: an owner of part of the company. Hold 10 of its 100 shares and you own 10% of it.

  • Shareholders usually get one vote per share, for example to choose the board of directors who make the big decisions for them.
  • Part of the profit may be paid out to them as a dividend.
  • Shares can be sold to someone else. The price of one share (the share price) rises when people expect the company to do well.

Selling new shares is a way for a company to raise money without borrowing it.

background.title: Borrowing, debts and who pays
background.html:
A business often needs money before it earns any. It can use the owners' savings, sell shares, or take a loan: borrowed money that must be paid back, plus interest, an extra charge each year (for example 8% of what is owed).

Money still owed is a debt. Things the business owns, such as machines, a van or cash, are its assets. If a business closes owing money, its assets are sold to pay the debts.

The big question in 1.2: if that is not enough, does the owner have to pay the rest from their own pocket? That is what liability is about.

background.title: Government, laws and taxes
background.html:
The government (also called the state) makes laws, collects taxes and uses the tax money for public services such as state schools and roads. Organisations it owns or controls are the public sector; everything owned by private people or firms is the private sector.

Laws set the minimum a business must do: keep workers safe, limit pollution, pay tax on its profit. Governments also try to attract businesses, for example with grants (money that is not paid back) or lower taxes, because businesses create jobs.

Choosing to do more than the law requires is corporate social responsibility (1.3).

background.title: How Business exam questions work
background.html:
Most IB Business questions are about a case study: a text about one business. The examiner wants you to use business ideas on that business, not in general.

  • The command term (the instruction word: define, explain, evaluate...) tells you how deep to go. Tap any command term on this page to see its official meaning.
  • The marks tell you how much to write: "explain two challenges [4 marks]" means two points worth 2 marks each.
  • Every point needs a fact or number from the case, then "this means... so...".

Long answers (10 marks) are marked with markbands: the examiner picks the level that best fits the whole answer.

terms.def: The instruction word in an exam question, such as explain or evaluate. It tells you what kind of answer the examiner wants and how deep to go.
IB command term (AO1): give the precise meaning of a word or idea.
IB command term (AO1): give a detailed account, that is, a full description of what something is or how it works.
IB command term (AO1): give a brief account or summary. Shorter than explain.
IB command term (AO2): give a detailed account including reasons or causes. Say what happens and why, linked to the case.
IB command term (AO2): use an idea or theory on a given problem, here the business in the case.
IB command term (AO3): weigh up the strengths and the limitations, then reach a judgement.
IB command term (AO3): give a balanced review with arguments on more than one side, and a clear conclusion backed by evidence.
IB command term (AO3): advise what the business should do, with evidence and reasons from the situation.
A text about one business, real or made up, that exam questions are based on. You must use its facts and numbers in your answers.
A short text the IB publishes before Paper 1: the start of the case study and some topics to research, so you know the background before the exam.
To do with numbers: calculations, data and tables.
One of the levels (1 to 2, 3 to 4 ... 9 to 10) used to mark a long answer. Each band has a description, and your answer gets the band it fits best.
Plural of formula: a rule written with words or letters and symbols, such as average cost = total cost ÷ output.
Methods (Unit 3) for deciding whether a big spend, such as a new machine, is worth it by comparing what it costs with what it will earn.
A comparison of two numbers. A staff-to-child ratio of 1 to 4 means one adult for every four children. In Unit 3, ratios compare figures from a firm's accounts.
The IB business management toolkit: a set of methods for analysing a business and making decisions, such as SWOT, STEEPLE and the business plan. You use them in every unit.
Backed up with evidence from the case and a clear chain of reasoning, not just stated.
Your final decision at the end of an evaluation, with the main reason and what it depends on: 'Yes, because..., but only if...'.
A weakness or missing piece in an argument or in the data, which means you cannot be fully sure. In a 10-mark answer: what the case does not tell you.
The things a business uses to make its product: materials, money, people's time and skills, machines and buildings.
Goods are physical things you can touch, such as a phone or a loaf. Services are things done for you, such as a haircut or a bus ride.
Two meanings. As a factor of production: man-made tools, machines and buildings. As money: what owners put into a business to start or grow it. 'More capital' on this page usually means more money.
The part of a business that deals with its people: hiring, training, pay and looking after staff. Often shortened to HR.

Money a business gets to start, run or grow, for example from the owner's savings, a bank loan or selling shares. 'Raising finance' means getting this money. As a business function (Unit 3), finance means managing the money.
The records of a business's money: what it sold, what it spent, its profit, and what it owns and owes. Companies must publish some of them for outsiders to see.
Everything a business does to find out what customers want and persuade them to buy: the product, its price, advertising and where it is sold.
The part of a business that makes the good or delivers the service: production, quality and stock.
What is left from the money coming in after all the costs are paid: profit = revenue − costs. If the costs are bigger, it is a loss.
All the money a business receives from selling its products, before any costs are taken off: price × number sold. Tax revenue is the money a government collects in taxes.
Bought from other businesses (suppliers), such as the coffee beans and cups a café buys.
The name, logo and image that make customers recognise a product and trust it. Branding is building that image so people choose it and may pay more.
All the making, buying, selling and working that goes on in a country or area.
A part of the economy. The four sectors (primary to quaternary) group businesses by the kind of work; the private and public sectors group them by who owns them.
When a country moves from mainly farming to mainly factories and manufacturing.
When manufacturing shrinks as a share of a country's jobs and output, and services grow instead.
A need that customers have and no business is meeting yet.
The group of customers a business aims its product at, for example students or young parents.
Interest is the extra a borrower pays for a loan, given as a percentage per year (the interest rate). Borrowing $6 000 at 10% costs about $600 a year.
A history of a firm's past sales and of paying its bills on time. Lenders use it to judge how risky a loan is.
The money moving into and out of a business over time. A cash flow problem means bills are due before customers have paid.
Money given by a government or organisation that does not have to be paid back.
Being legally responsible for something, especially for paying debts. If you are liable for a debt, you can be made to pay it.
Things of value that a business or person owns, such as buildings, machines, cash or a car.
A person or organisation that owns shares in a company, so owns part of it. They vote on big decisions and may receive dividends.
Equal parts of a company's ownership. If a company has 100 shares and you hold 10, you own 10% of it.
The type of business the law recognises, such as sole trader, partnership or company. It decides who owns the business and who must pay its debts.
In business, 'the state' means the government. State-owned means owned by the government.
Money left over after all costs are paid. In a non-profit organisation it is called a surplus, not profit, because none of it goes to owners.
Set up to make a profit. A for-profit social enterprise makes a profit but uses most of it for its social aim.
Not run to make money for owners. It can still earn money, but any surplus goes back into its purpose.
When one company buys control of another (more than half its shares) even though the other company's managers do not want it. More in 1.5.
A market where shares in publicly held companies are bought and sold, such as the London Stock Exchange.
To invest is to put money into something, such as shares, machines or a new shop, hoping to get more back later. Investors are people or firms who do this.
Put back into the business or its cause instead of being paid out to owners.
Any person or group who affects, or is affected by, what a business does, such as staff, customers, suppliers and the local community. Explained in 1.4.
Falls in the cost of making each item when a business produces more, for example from buying in bulk. Explained in 1.5.
One firm's sales as a percentage of all sales in its market. If customers buy 100 bikes and 30 are yours, your market share is 30%. The firm with the biggest share is the market leader.
The people at the top of an organisation, such as directors, who make the big long-term decisions. Their jobs are the senior jobs.
What one share of a company costs to buy right now. It rises when investors expect the company to do well.
The part of a company's profit paid out to its shareholders: the same amount for each share they own, so someone with more shares gets more. The amount can change from year to year.
All the firms and steps involved in getting a product to the customer, from raw materials to the shop.
A period when a country's economy shrinks: people spend less, firms sell less and more people lose their jobs.
Places where a business sells its products, such as shops, cafés or branches.
An organised group that campaigns to change what businesses or governments do on one issue, such as the environment or animal welfare.
Making a business look more environmentally friendly than it really is, through adverts or claims not backed by action.
What a person or group wants or cares about. Employees' interests include fair pay and job security. 'In the interests of society' means for the good of society.
Extra pay for staff that goes up when the firm's profit goes up.
A plan that gives or sells staff shares in the company they work for, so they gain when it does well.
The everyday costs of running a business, such as wages, rent, energy and transport.
For each single item made. Unit cost is the cost of making one item, the same as average cost.
All the firms that make the same kind of product, for example the car industry or the software industry.
Levels of management between the top of the business and the workers. More layers means a message passes through more people.

A firm's culture is the shared values and ways of working of its people: 'how we do things here'. A culture clash is when two firms with different cultures are joined. Local culture means a country's way of life.
The board of directors: a small group chosen by the shareholders to make a company's biggest decisions and keep watch on its managers.
A small, specialised part of a market with particular needs, for example left-handed guitars.
A period when a government lets a business pay little or no tax, to persuade it to set up in the country.
Something that encourages a person to act in a certain way, such as extra pay for hard work.
IB command term (AO2): make clear the differences between two or more ideas or things. For example: private sector is owned by private people, public sector by the government.

Assessment objective: how deep the IB goes on a topic. AO1: know and describe. AO2: explain and apply to a case. AO3: evaluate, discuss or recommend (weigh up and judge). AO4: calculate and use skills.
A toolkit tool that lists the outside factors that can affect a business: social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and ethical.
In business, demand is how much of a product customers want to buy and can pay for. Weekend queues show high demand. As a verb, to demand something is to insist on it: 'the law does not demand it'.
To find and hire new staff.
An organisation that does business. 'Types of business entities' means the different kinds: sole traders, partnerships, companies, cooperatives and NGOs.
A factory that processes crude oil (oil as it comes out of the ground) into petrol, diesel and other products.
A plant is a large factory. A car plant (or assembly plant) puts cars together from their parts.
To bear a cost or loss is to carry it or suffer it. 'The lenders bear the rest' means the banks that lent the money lose it.
Ask people for their views before you decide, so they feel heard and you learn their worries.
In large amounts at once. Suppliers often give a lower price per item for a big order: a bulk discount.
People who want a job but cannot find one. Youth unemployment means young people without jobs.
Bought from another country and brought in. Imported parts are made abroad, so local suppliers get no orders for them.
The examiner's list of what earns each mark for a question, sometimes with sample answers. You use it to mark your own work.
The first part of Business Papers 1 and 2: questions split into parts, such as (a) and (b), marked point by point. Section B holds the 10-mark answer.
Officially checked and approved by an independent organisation, for example as paying its workers fairly.
The main office of a company, where the top managers work and the big decisions are made.
A written agreement that the law can enforce, such as the rules a franchisee must follow.
Keeping food, hands and places clean so that people do not get ill.
Information and communication technology: computers, software, data and the internet.
Making goods in factories from materials or parts, for example cars or chocolate bars.
Building houses, offices, roads and bridges.
Gases sent into the air, such as carbon dioxide from burning fuel, which add to pollution and climate change.
In your teacher's 10-mark guide: a sentence saying when the argument is stronger or weaker, such as 'However, this depends on...'. Not a certificate.
An angry feeling of being treated unfairly.
Customers who buy a lot less when the price goes up even a little.
